screens.title: Libraries and Upgradable Contracts
screens.subtitle: Reuse logic with libraries and evolve contracts safely with proxy patterns

narration.text: In this lesson we study two practical tools used in Solidity: libraries for reuse and proxy-based upgradability for controlled evolution. Libraries let you bundle stateless utility functions and deploy them once, reducing duplicated bytecode across contracts. When called with delegate behavior, a library runs in the caller's context so it operates on the calling contract's storage and preserves msg. sender and msg. value. That makes libraries compact and gas-friendly, and the using for directive lets library functions feel like methods on a type. Upgradability addresses the immutable nature of deployed contracts. By separating state from logic—holding data in a proxy and forwarding calls to a replaceable implementation—you can change behavior without losing stored balances or configuration. There are several proxy styles, such as Transparent and UUPS, each with different trade-offs around who can upgrade and where the upgrade logic lives. However, upgradability introduces complexity and risks like storage collisions or unauthorized upgrades, so it should be chosen deliberately and protected with audited upgrade tooling. As we move through examples and code demos, notice how library calls and delegatecall interact with storage, and reflect on whether you want a changing contract in production or prefer immutable guarantees.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Libraries reduce duplicated bytecode and improve gas costs; proxies let logic change while preserving state, but they require careful security design.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why Solidity libraries are used and how they reduce code duplication and gas costs. You will practice attaching a library to a type using the using for directive so you can call utility functions like methods on variables. You will understand why delegate semantics matter: when library code runs in the caller context it operates on the caller's storage and preserves the caller identity and value transfers. You will also be able to describe the core problem that upgradable contracts address — immutable deployed code — and explain how a proxy separates state from logic to allow upgrades without losing stored data. Finally, you will learn the differences between popular proxy styles and identify security risks such as storage collisions and improper access control. These skills let you make deliberate design decisions, choose when to use libraries for reuse and gas savings, and when to adopt an upgrade pattern while applying appropriate safeguards.

screens.title: What is a Solidity Library?
screens.subtitle: Definition, state behavior, and deployment model

narration.text: A Solidity library is a special contract used to package reusable functions, typically stateless utilities that multiple contracts can call. The library itself is deployed once at a fixed address; other contracts reference that address rather than duplicating code. When a library function is invoked via delegate-style semantics, the library code executes in the context of the calling contract. That means the storage layout, msg. sender, and msg. value referenced by the library are those of the caller, not the library contract. This is why libraries are frequently stateless: they operate on the caller's state. The single-deployment model reduces bytecode duplication and can lower gas costs because multiple contracts share the same library implementation. A common misconception is to treat libraries like ordinary contracts with independent storage: when delegate execution is used they do not have their own persistent state in that scenario. Use libraries for utilities such as string helpers, arithmetic helpers, or data structure manipulation. As you write code, prefer attaching functions with the using for directive when it improves readability, and remember delegate semantics when your library reads or writes storage.

keyIdea.title: Library definition
keyIdea.text: A deployed, reusable contract whose functions can run in the caller's context to save bytecode and gas; not a separate storage owner when used via delegate semantics.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is a Library?
Definition

Solidity Library essentials

A library packages reusable functions, is deployed once, and can execute in a caller's context so it operates on the caller's storage and identity.

Behavior note
When called via delegate semantics the library has no independent storage; it uses the caller's state.
Benefit
Deploy once and reuse to reduce bytecode duplication and lower gas across many contracts.
Common misconception
Thinking a library keeps its own storage when used with delegatecall. In reality the caller's storage is used.
Concrete example
StringUtils library
// isEmpty and concatenate functions
library StringUtils {
  function isEmpty(string memory s) internal pure returns (bool) {
    return bytes(s).length == 0;
  }
  function concatenate(string memory a, string memory b) internal pure returns (string memory) {
    return string(abi.encodePacked(a, b));
  }
}
Key takeaway

Libraries let you write once and reference from many contracts; when delegate semantics are involved, library code acts on the caller's state and identity.

screens.title: CALL vs DELEGATECALL for Libraries
screens.subtitle: How invocation choices change execution context

narration.text: Library functions can be invoked in two main ways from the perspective of callers: as external calls or with delegate-style execution. An external CALL runs the library code in the library's own context: it uses the library's storage and sees library msg. sender values. This is appropriate for truly independent contracts. In contrast, DELEGATECALL executes code from the target address but within the calling contract's context. When you use delegate-style semantics or using for that relies on delegate-like behavior, any storage reads and writes operate on the caller's storage layout; msg. sender and msg. value reflect the original caller who invoked the top-level transaction. The practical effect is significant: delegate execution allows utility code to manipulate the caller's data without copying storage definitions, enabling compact, reusable helpers. A common mistake is to mix storage assumptions across library and caller without explicit slot coordination. Always design library routines to operate on primitive inputs or carefully documented storage slots if they must touch contract state. CALL vs DELEGATECALL for Libraries means call isolates execution in library context; delegatecall runs library code inside the caller's storage and preserves original caller identity.. In practical terms, how invocation choices change execution context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Invocation contrast
keyIdea.text: CALL isolates execution in library context; DELEGATECALL runs library code inside the caller's storage and preserves original caller identity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › CALL vs DELEGATECALL
Comparison

CALL (external) vs DELEGATECALL (delegate)

  • CALL: runs in callee's context, uses callee storage and sees callee msg.sender.
  • DELEGATECALL: runs callee code in caller context, using caller storage and original msg.sender and msg.value.
  • Use when: CALL for independent modules; DELEGATECALL for library-style helpers that operate on caller state.
  • Misconception: thinking both are interchangeable—storage and identity semantics differ and matter for safety.
Pro tip

If a library reads or writes state, prefer delegate semantics and document the expected storage layout or avoid storage writes entirely.

Visual summary
CALL
Library has independent context; safe for isolated utilities.
Storage: library's. Identity: library sees its own msg.sender as the caller.
DELEGATECALL
Library code runs as if it were part of the caller contract.
Storage: caller's. Identity: original tx sender preserved.
Example implication

When using delegate semantics, the library's logic can update balances stored in the caller without the caller including that code in its bytecode.

screens.title: `using for` and method-like library calls
screens.subtitle: Attach library functions to types for clearer code

narration.text: The using for directive in Solidity attaches library functions to a target type so you can call them with method-like syntax. This is syntactic sugar that improves readability and reduces errors. For example, after using String Utils for string. you can call underscore input. is Empty open parenthesis close parenthesis instead of String Utils. is Empty open parenthesis underscore input close parenthesis. The directive does not change runtime semantics: when functions are implemented as internal or use delegate-style behavior, they still execute with the caller context if designed that way. A concrete example is a text-processing contract that stores a greeting and uses library methods to check and concatenate strings. This makes the code easy to follow for future maintainers. One common misuse is applying using for to types when the library actually changes storage slots in ways the caller does not expect. To avoid that, keep library methods pure or clearly document any storage interactions. As you implement using for in exercises, prefer pure helpers for data transformation and leave stateful behaviors to intentionally designed upgradeable modules. `using for` and method-like library calls means `using for` creates method-like access to library functions and improves readability while preserving execution semantics.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › `using for` Demo
Code Walkthrough

StringUtils + using for

Library
library StringUtils {
  function isEmpty(string memory s) internal pure returns (bool) {
    return bytes(s).length == 0;
  }
  function concatenate(string memory a, string memory b) internal pure returns (string memory) {
    return string(abi.encodePacked(a, b));
  }
}
Contract using it
contract MyTextProcessor {
  using StringUtils for string;
  string public greeting = "Hello";
  function processAndDisplay(string memory inp) public view returns (string memory) {
    if (inp.isEmpty()) {
      return greeting.concatenate(" World!");
    } else {
      return greeting.concatenate(" ").concatenate(inp);
    }
  }
}
Example result

Calling processAndDisplay with an empty input returns "Hello World!" since isEmpty triggers the concatenate fallback.

Watch out

Avoid attaching libraries that implicitly assume a particular storage layout.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › SafeMath Task
Hands-on

SafeMath + Calculator

SafeMath library
library SafeMath {
  function add(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    uint256 c = a + b;
    require(c >= a, "SafeMath: addition overflow");
    return c;
  }
  function sub(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    require(b <= a, "SafeMath: subtraction underflow");
    return a - b;
  }
}
Calculator contract
contract Calculator {
  using SafeMath for uint256;
  uint256 public result;
  constructor(uint256 initialValue) { result = initialValue; }
  function addNumbers(uint256 v) public { result = result.add(v); }
  function subtractNumbers(uint256 v) public { result = result.sub(v); }
  function getResult() public view returns (uint256) { return result; }
}
Try this

Deploy the library and contract locally, call addNumbers and subtractNumbers, and verify getResult preserves expected values even after revert attempts.

Common error

Forgetting to link or deploy the library address when external linking is required in older Solidity workflows.

screens.title: Why upgradable contracts?
screens.subtitle: The immutability challenge and a pragmatic solution

narration.text: Immutability is a fundamental property of deployed contracts: once code is on-chain it's fixed. That provides integrity and predictability, but it makes bug fixes and feature additions difficult. Upgradable contracts address that problem by separating persistent state from the contract logic that implements behavior. In the proxy pattern, an immutable proxy stores the state and delegates execution to a separate implementation contract. Upgrades happen by deploying a new logic contract and updating the proxy to point to the new implementation. This preserves state like balances or owner settings while changing behavior. The trade-off is a loss of the strict 'code is law' guarantee, because the contract's behavior can change over time if the upgrade path is not tightly controlled. Decide to use upgradability only when you need long-lived flexibility, and secure the upgrade mechanism with access control and audited tooling. A practical example is fixing a discovered bug or adding a new feature without migrating user data off-chain. Why upgradable contracts? means upgrades let you change logic without losing state, at the cost of added complexity and a need for careful governance and security controls.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Why Upgradable?
Definition

Upgradable Contracts explained

Upgradability separates state and logic so you can replace the code that implements behavior while preserving stored data.

Typical flow
Deploy proxy with state, deploy implementation with logic, point proxy to implementation, update pointer to upgrade.
Why use it
Fix bugs, add features, or change behavior without moving user data off-chain or requiring complex migrations.
Trade-off
Upgradable design increases complexity and introduces risks that must be mitigated through governance and testing.
Scenario
Fixing a bug without migration

If a deployed token reveals a rounding bug, an upgrade can fix transfer logic while leaving user balances intact in the proxy's storage.

Key takeaway

Upgradability is a pragmatic tool for long-lived systems, but adopt it only with strong governance and audited libraries.

screens.title: Proxy Pattern Architecture
screens.subtitle: Proxy contract holds state; implementation holds logic

narration.text: The proxy pattern has two primary actors: the proxy contract and the implementation contract. The proxy is a minimal, typically immutable contract that stores state variables — balances, ownership, configuration — and forwards function calls to an implementation contract. Forwarding is commonly done with delegatecall so that the implementation code runs using the proxy's storage. The implementation contract contains the business logic: transfer, mint, process a transaction. When you upgrade, you deploy a new implementation and update the proxy's pointer to it. In Transparent proxies, the proxy owner has special administrative functions that are executed on the proxy and are not forwarded to the implementation for normal users. In UUPS the upgrade logic itself lives inside the implementation, and the proxy remains a simple forwarding layer. When designing the storage layout, you must ensure the implementation's variables map to the proxy's storage slots to avoid storage collisions. A clear separation of responsibilities and careful storage planning are central to a correct proxy architecture. In practical terms, proxy contract holds state; implementation holds logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Proxy Architecture
Architecture

Proxy ← delegatecall ← Implementation

The proxy holds the state and forwards calls to an implementation that contains the logic. Using delegatecall allows the implementation's code to operate on proxy storage.

Proxy
Holds state and the pointer to the implementation address.
Implementation
Contains functions like transfer and mint; replaceable for upgrades.
Delegatecall
Executes implementation code in proxy's context so storage and msg.sender are preserved.
Checklist
  • Design storage layout and reserve slots for proxy-specific variables.
  • Minimize proxy complexity; prefer audited upgrade helpers.
  • Restrict who can perform upgrades with strong access control.
Misconception

The proxy is not a full duplication of logic — it intentionally delegates to keep the forwarding layer small and stateful.

screens.title: Transparent Proxy vs UUPS
screens.subtitle: Two common upgrade patterns and their trade-offs

narration.text: Two frequently used proxy approaches are the Transparent Proxy Pattern and the UUPS pattern. The Transparent proxy keeps upgrade logic and administrative controls at the proxy level. It distinguishes between calls from the admin and regular users: admin calls execute proxy administrative functions while normal user calls are forwarded to the implementation. This separation can reduce surprises but requires careful admin checks. UUPS places the upgrade mechanism inside the implementation contract itself. The proxy becomes a minimal forwarding layer, and the implementation exposes an upgrade function that, when called by an authorized actor, updates the pointer stored by the proxy. UUPS can lead to smaller proxies and more flexible deployment flows, but it requires discipline: since the upgrade logic resides in implementation code, any bug in the implementation could affect upgradeability. The practical choice depends on governance preferences, desire for minimal proxy code, and how you want to manage administrative responsibilities. Transparent Proxy vs UUPS means transparent proxies centralize admin at the proxy, uups places upgrade logic in the implementation; choose based on governance and risk appetite.. In practical terms, two common upgrade patterns and their trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Transparent proxies centralize admin at the proxy, UUPS places upgrade logic in the implementation; choose based on governance and risk appetite.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Transparent vs UUPS
Transparent Proxy

Proxy-level admin

Admin functions live at the proxy. Calls from the admin are handled differently than user calls, preventing conflicts with implementation functions.

Good for well-defined admin separation and simple upgrade governance.
Requires the proxy to implement admin controls and careful access checks.
UUPS

Implementation-level upgrade logic

The implementation holds the upgrade function, while the proxy remains a thin forwarder. Upgrades are invoked through the implementation's logic and then update the proxy's pointer.

Leads to smaller proxies and flexible deployment but requires secure implementation code for upgrade paths.
A buggy implementation could compromise upgrade mechanisms, so auditing is essential.
Decision guide

Choose Transparent when you want admin separation at the proxy. Choose UUPS for a minimal proxy and when you accept upgrade logic living in implementation code with rigorous testing.

screens.title: Delegatecall mechanics in proxies
screens.subtitle: How msg.sender, msg.value, and storage behave during forwarding

narration.text: Delegatecall is the key EVM mechanism that makes proxies work. When the proxy uses delegatecall to forward a function invocation, the implementation's bytecode executes as if it were part of the proxy contract. That means storage reads and writes operate on the proxy's storage slots. Crucially, msg. sender inside the implementation reflects the original caller of the transaction, not the proxy address. Likewise, msg. value representing attached value is preserved through delegatecall so the implementation can rely on payment context. This behavior lets the implementation manipulate persistent state held by the proxy and rely on the correct transaction sender for access checks. A frequent misconception is that delegatecall changes who the caller is — it does not. However, delegatecall also means the implementation's declared storage layout must align with the proxy's layout; otherwise you risk storage collisions. In practice, the process of forwarding is: user calls proxy, proxy delegatecalls implementation with calldata, implementation runs using proxy storage and original msg. sender, result is returned to proxy and relayed back to caller. Understanding this sequence is essential for safe upgrades. Delegatecall mechanics in proxies means delegatecall executes implementation logic in proxy context, preserving original msg.sender and msg.value while using proxy storage.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Delegatecall Mechanics
Step-by-step

Forwarding sequence with delegatecall

1. User call

User sends a transaction to the proxy with calldata and possibly value.

2. Proxy forwards

Proxy uses delegatecall with the implementation address and forwards calldata.

3. Implementation runs

Implementation code executes using proxy storage; msg.sender is the original caller and msg.value is preserved.

4. Return

Implementation returns to proxy, which returns to the user. State changes are stored in the proxy.

Storage collision risk

If the implementation declares variables in a different order than the proxy, reads and writes may touch the wrong slots and corrupt state.

Practical check

Reserve storage slots for proxy administration and document expected layout for implementation contracts.

screens.title: Storage collisions and upgrade hazards
screens.subtitle: Why variable layout matters during upgrades

narration.text: Storage collisions are one of the most serious hazards in upgradable contract design. They occur when the proxy's storage layout and the implementation's declared variables do not align, so a variable written by the implementation maps to the wrong storage slot in the proxy. This can corrupt balances, ownership flags, or configuration values. The underlying cause is that delegatecall uses the proxy's storage slots, and implementations are compiled with their own assumed slot ordering. To avoid collisions, reserve slots in the proxy for essential administration data, keep a consistent variable ordering across implementations, or use explicit slot-based storage patterns. Another hazard is unauthorized upgrades: if upgrade controls are weak, an attacker or mistaken key-holder could point the proxy at malicious logic. Use strong access control and audited tooling for upgrade operations. Finally, treat upgradability as a governance decision: document who can upgrade, why upgrades might be performed, and how to revert or migrate if needed. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Storage collisions
Security focus

Storage collisions and mitigation

A storage collision happens when storage slots assumed by the implementation do not match the proxy's actual layout. Because delegatecall uses proxy storage, mismatches corrupt state.

Reserve dedicated slots in the proxy for admin data and document them.
Keep variable ordering stable or use explicit slot storage helpers to avoid implicit reordering problems.
Use audited upgrade plugins and limit upgrade authority to a secure governance process.
Example pitfall
Adding a new variable earlier

If an implementation adds a new state variable at the top of its contract, subsequent variables shift slots and can map to proxy state meant for different data.

Warning

Never change storage layout lightly; treat storage compatibility as a top-level design requirement.

screens.title: Secure upgrade practices
screens.subtitle: Access control, audits, and tooling recommendations

narration.text: Secure upgrades require a combination of process, code hygiene, and tooling. First, lock upgrade authority behind strict access control: limit who can change the implementation pointer and prefer multisig or governance contracts rather than single-key ownership. Second, adopt battle-tested libraries and upgrade plugins that provide standardized, audited upgrade flows and help prevent common mistakes. Third, prioritize storage compatibility: define and freeze storage slots used by the proxy, and document any reserved slots so future implementations maintain alignment. Fourth, test upgrade flows on non-production networks and simulate malicious upgrade attempts to verify controls. Finally, communicate upgrade policies to users: let them know when the contract may change and how governance will approve modifications. A common error is trusting unreviewed upgrade logic; always audit both implementation and upgrade pathways. These practices balance flexibility with security and help teams use upgradability responsibly. Secure upgrade practices means use strict access control, audited upgrade tools, documented storage slots, and testing to make upgrades safe and accountable.. Best practices

Securing upgrade paths

Access control

Prefer multisig or governance contracts to single keys for performing upgrades; record who can upgrade and how.

Audited tooling

Rely on battle-tested upgrade plugins and audited libraries to manage pointers and migrations safely.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's recap the essential ideas. First, a library is a reusable contract deployed once; when its code is executed in a caller context via delegate semantics it operates on the caller's storage and preserves msg. sender and msg. value. Second, the using for directive attaches library functions to a type to let you call them as methods, improving readability and maintainability. Third, upgradable contracts separate state and logic using a proxy and implementation pattern so logic can evolve without losing stored data. Keep in mind the security implications: storage collisions can corrupt state when layouts diverge, and upgrade controls must be restricted. Choose between Transparent and UUPS based on governance and where you want upgrade logic to live. Use audited tooling, document storage slots, and test upgrade paths. These points will help you use libraries for code reuse and apply upgradability only when the trade-offs justify it.

keyIdea.title: Concise takeaway

Libraries improve reuse and gas efficiency; proxies enable upgrades but require storage planning, governance, and audited tools to be safe.

narration.text: Finish with three concise reminders. First, delegatecall preserves the original caller and value while executing code in the caller's storage context — that property enables proxies and library delegate semantics. Second, storage layout compatibility is non-negotiable for upgrades: document reserved slots and avoid reordering state variables. Third, treat upgrades as a governance and security decision: use audited upgrade tooling, enforce strict access control, and test upgrade paths thoroughly. These three rules help you get the benefits of reuse and evolution while minimizing catastrophic risks.
